stem:
A 58-year-old man spent two decades cutting engineered stone worktops with a dry-cutting saw and rarely wore a mask. He now has several years of gradually worsening exertional breathlessness and a dry cough. A chest X-ray shows multiple small rounded nodules, most dense in the upper zones, with enlarged hilar nodes.

Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.E: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis of unknown cause

correct_answer: A. Silicosis from inhaled crystalline dust
why_correct: Engineered stone is very rich in crystalline silica, and years of dry cutting expose workers to respirable silica dust. This causes silicosis, a fibrotic pneumoconiosis with small nodules concentrated in the upper zones and enlarged hilar nodes. Prevention depends on controlling dust at source and wearing respiratory protection, and affected workers should be removed from further exposure. Source: UK Health and Safety Executive guidance on respirable crystalline silica; standard respiratory teaching (HSE pages not fetched for this item).
why_wrong: B. Asbestosis causes lower-zone fibrosis with pleural plaques, not upper-zone nodules after stone dust exposure. C. Byssinosis follows cotton, flax or hemp dust and presents as chest tightness on the first working day of the week. D. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis follows repeated inhalation of organic antigens such as bird protein and does not fit this occupation. E. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis causes basal subpleural fibrosis with no identifiable exposure.
pearl: Think silicosis in anyone who cuts, drills or blasts stone, brick, concrete or engineered stone, and remember that it also raises the risk of tuberculosis and lung cancer.
thinking: Years of dry-cutting engineered stone  ↓  Chronic breathlessness with upper-zone nodules and hilar nodes  ↓  Pneumoconiosis from crystalline silica  ↓  Silicosis
exam_trap: Choosing asbestosis because it is the best-known occupational lung disease, when the exposure here is stone dust and the nodules are upper zone rather than lower zone.
takeaway: Stone, sand or engineered-stone dust with upper-zone nodules points to silicosis.
notes: Adapted from N4515 (silica worker with upper-lobe nodular disease). No live repeat found: DT120 concerns TB complicating silicosis (different learning point); asbestos items RES024/PAAKT025/PAQ15445 are pleural. Source key correct. Angle changed: exposure disguised as engineered-stone cutting (named hazard in UK practice) so the candidate must infer silica. No guideline fetched; cited as standard teaching.
Duplicate of PAN1748 (prescribe oxygen to a target saturation range suited to the patient; same key, same distractors) and PAN244 (94-98% target); also RES045/BX933 for 88-92%.
Duplicate of PAN1748 (prescribe oxygen to a target range; same learning point) and PAN244.
Duplicate of PAN1748 (target-saturation principle for oxygen) and PAN244; same learning point as the other oxygen items in this batch.
Duplicate: severe COPD with raised JVP, oedema and hepatomegaly leading to cor pulmonale is live in RES035 and PAQ594.
Duplicate: cor pulmonale as right heart failure from chronic lung disease is live in RES035 and PAQ594 (same key).

stem:
An 82-year-old man with known heart failure stopped taking his furosemide two weeks ago. He is admitted with orthopnoea, weight gain and leg swelling but no fever or chest pain. A chest X-ray shows cardiomegaly with moderate bilateral pleural effusions of similar size.

What is the most appropriate approach to the effusions?

options.A: Bilateral ultrasound-guided aspiration now to exclude malignancy
options.B: Bilateral intercostal drains to relieve his breathlessness
options.C: Treat the heart failure with diuretics and review progress
options.D: Intravenous antibiotics for a presumed pleural infection
options.E: Referral for talc pleurodesis on both sides

correct_answer: C. Treat the heart failure with diuretics and review progress
why_correct: Symmetrical bilateral effusions in a patient with decompensated heart failure and no atypical features are presumed to be transudates. The best approach is to treat the underlying heart failure with diuretics and review the response. Pleural sampling is reserved for effusions that are unilateral or asymmetrical, associated with pleuritic pain or fever, or that fail to resolve with treatment. Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guideline 2023; standard teaching (guideline page not fetched).
why_wrong: A. Routine aspiration of both sides exposes him to risk without benefit when the clinical picture is clearly heart failure and there are no atypical features. B. Drains are for pleural infection, large symptomatic effusions or pneumothorax, and are not first-line for a transudate that will respond to diuretics. D. There is no fever, pleuritic pain or consolidation to suggest empyema. E. Pleurodesis is for recurrent malignant effusions, not for fluid from heart failure.
pearl: Treat first and tap later in bilateral effusions with clear heart failure, but sample if the effusion is unilateral, asymmetrical or fails to respond.
thinking: Stopped diuretic, orthopnoea and oedema  ↓  Bilateral similar-sized effusions, no fever or pain  ↓  Presumed transudate  ↓  Diuretics and reassess
exam_trap: Aspirating or draining both sides by reflex, when the clinical context makes a transudate likely and treatment of the cause should come first.
takeaway: Bilateral effusions in decompensated heart failure are managed by treating the heart failure.
notes: Adapted from N1946 (generic 'treat underlying cause'). Source stem was vague; angle sharpened to a decompensated-HF vignette with explicit atypical-feature caveat (unilateral, fever, pleuritic pain, non-response) per BTS teaching. Not a repeat of BX266 (diagnosis) or Light's items. Same vignette family as PAN4490 but different learning point (management vs mechanism). Guideline cited as standard teaching, not fetched.
Duplicate: asbestos exposure with pleural effusion pointing to mesothelioma is live in RES024 and PAAKT025 (diagnosis re-skins).

stem:
A 77-year-old woman has long-standing heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and is increasingly breathless on exertion, with swollen ankles. Percussion is stony dull at both lung bases, with reduced breath sounds, and a chest X-ray shows an enlarged heart with small effusions of similar size on both sides. She has no fever or pleuritic pain.

Which mechanism best explains the pleural fluid?

options.A: Obstruction of a main bronchus by an endobronchial tumour
options.B: Spread of bacteria from the adjacent lung into the pleura
options.C: Leakage of lymph from a damaged thoracic duct
options.D: Increased capillary permeability from pleural inflammation
options.E: Raised capillary pressure forcing fluid into the pleura

correct_answer: E. Raised capillary pressure forcing fluid into the pleura
why_correct: In heart failure the raised venous and pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure drives protein-poor fluid across the pleural membranes faster than the lymphatics can clear it. This produces a transudate, typically bilateral and roughly symmetrical. Inflammatory, infective and malignant effusions are exudates and usually unilateral or asymmetrical. Source: BTS Pleural Disease Guideline 2023; standard teaching (guideline page not fetched).
why_wrong: A. Bronchial obstruction causes lung collapse and may be associated with a unilateral malignant effusion, not symmetrical bilateral fluid in heart failure. B. Bacterial spread produces a parapneumonic effusion or empyema, which needs fever and a lung infection. C. Thoracic duct leakage causes a chylothorax, usually after trauma, surgery or lymphoma. D. Increased permeability from inflammation produces an exudate, whereas here there is no pleuritic pain, fever or inflammatory trigger.
pearl: Bilateral, symmetrical effusions in a patient with clear heart failure are almost always transudates caused by hydrostatic pressure.
thinking: Known heart failure with bilateral basal dullness  ↓  Symmetrical effusions, no fever or pleuritic pain  ↓  Transudate  ↓  Raised hydrostatic pressure
exam_trap: Choosing increased capillary permeability, which describes exudates (infection, malignancy, inflammation) rather than the pressure-driven transudate of heart failure.
takeaway: Heart failure causes bilateral transudative effusions through raised hydrostatic pressure.
notes: Adapted from N4490. Source option E 'Pulmonary embolism in every case' was an absolute-wording distractor; replaced with plausible mechanism distractors. Not a repeat of BX266 (diagnosis of effusion from signs) or Light's criteria items RES018/RES031/CR062/PAAKT020 (exudate classification). Pleural guideline cited as standard teaching; BTS/Thorax sites returned bot-block, so not verified by fetch.
Duplicate: pleuritic pain with tachycardia and hypoxaemia leading to Wells pathway is live in ACU020 (key: calculate Wells score then D-dimer or CTPA) and RES041.
Duplicate: CTPA as the PE imaging test is live in CR024 (Wells 5, key CTPA) and ACU020; also BX550/OG059.
Duplicate: DVT as the source of PE with a swollen leg is live in BX144 and PAN6954 (DVT/PE linkage) and GF014.
Duplicate: negative D-dimer to exclude PE in low-probability patient is live in RES041, BX549 and PAQ1116.
Duplicate: CURB65 severity of confused, hypotensive, tachypnoeic pneumonia is live in ID019, ID044 and Q357 (same CURB65 inputs).
Duplicate: confusion, hypotension and tachypnoea as severe pneumonia needing urgent assessment is live in ID019 and ID044 (high CURB65, admit as severe).
Duplicate: parapneumonic effusion/pleural fluid complicating pneumonia is live in DR092 (day 4 pneumonia plus effusion, key diagnostic aspiration), RES048, DR093, PAAKT150 and BX267.
Duplicate: pus in pleural space as empyema is live in BX267 (frank pus, key empyema) plus DR093, RES048 and PAAKT150.

stem:
A 69-year-old man has had 3 days of fever, productive cough and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. A chest X-ray confirms right lower lobe consolidation. He is alert and orientated, with a temperature of 38.9°C, pulse 104/min, respiratory rate 22/min, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 93% on air. His C-reactive protein is markedly raised. The admitting doctor calculates his CURB65 score.

Which of his findings contributes a point to the score?

options.A: His age of 69 years, over the cut-off
options.C: A resting pulse rate of 104 beats per minute
options.E: A markedly raised C-reactive protein level

correct_answer: A. His age of 69 years, over the cut-off
why_correct: CURB65 gives one point each for new confusion, urea above 7 mmol/L, respiratory rate of 30 or more, low blood pressure (systolic under 90 or diastolic 60 or less) and age 65 or over. This man is alert, with a respiratory rate of 22 and normal blood pressure, so only his age scores, and his urea is not yet known. Fever, tachycardia, pleuritic pain and CRP are not part of the score, so clinical judgement and oxygen saturation must be used alongside it. Source: NICE NG250 Pneumonia: diagnosis and management, 2025 (Box 2, CURB65).
why_wrong: B. Temperature is not a CURB65 component, although it supports infection. C. Heart rate is not part of CURB65 even though it is in NEWS2. D. Pleuritic pain is a feature of lobar pneumonia but does not score. E. CRP helps confirm infection and guide treatment decisions but is not in the score.
pearl: CURB65 is Confusion, Urea, Respiratory rate, Blood pressure and age 65 or over, and fever, pulse, saturation and CRP are not in it.
thinking: Consolidation on X-ray in a 69-year-old  ↓  Check each CURB65 item  ↓  Alert, RR 22, BP normal  ↓  Only age scores
exam_trap: Counting the fever, pulse or CRP because they look abnormal, although none of them is a CURB65 component.
takeaway: CURB65 uses confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure and age 65 or over, and nothing else.
notes: Adapted from N10448 (bare recall: which factor is in CURB-65). Built a vignette so candidate must pick the scoring finding from several abnormal ones. Source key correct; verified against NICE NG250 (published 2 September 2025) Box 2, which keeps the 2014 CURB65 definition. Not a repeat of Q357 (score calculation), ID019/ID044 (interpretation of a high score). PAN10449 (RR component) skipped as same learning point within this batch. Urea intentionally not given.
Skipped: same learning point as PAN10448 (CURB65 components) already written in this batch; respiratory-rate threshold is also covered by Q357/ID019/ID044 inputs.
